opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the most exciting part of robotics has always been the intersection between learning and decision-making: how do we get robots to not just perceive the world, but actually reason about it and act over long horizons? Early on I was drawn to computer vision, but I quickly realized that seeing isn't enough. A robot has to understand what it can *do* with what it sees, and how a sequence of actions leads toward a goal.

So a lot of what I care about is long-horizon manipulation. Think about something like cooking a meal or tidying up a kitchen. Those tasks involve dozens of steps, lots of objects, and constant adaptation when things don't go as planned. Classical planning gives you structure and composability, and deep learning gives you flexibility and the ability to deal with raw sensory input. I find it really interesting to figure out how to combine those two, so the robot can learn skills from data but also compose them in a structured way to solve new problems it's never seen before.

The other piece I'm passionate about is data. Unlike language or vision, robotics doesn't have an internet-scale dataset lying around. So questions like: how do we collect demonstrations efficiently, how do we learn from humans, how do we use simulation, and how do we make the most of every bit of data we have? To me, that's one of the central bottlenecks in the field right now, and solving it is what will eventually get robots out of the lab and into people's homes in a useful way.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The part that interests me most is the gap between what a robot can do in a controlled demo and what it can do in a real, messy environment. I spent a lot of my early work on perception and planning, and I kept running into the same wall: you can get a system to pick up a cup on a clean table, but the moment the lighting changes or someone leaves a backpack on the counter, everything falls apart. That fragility is what pulled me toward learning-based approaches, and specifically toward how robots can learn from humans.

So the thing I find myself most excited about now is imitation learning and the broader question of how you get data into a robot. Humans are incredibly good at demonstrating tasks, but demonstrations are expensive, and a few hundred examples won't cover the variety a robot sees in a kitchen or a warehouse. I'm interested in how we stretch that data: how a robot can take a handful of demonstrations and generalize to new objects, new layouts, longer tasks that chain many steps together. That connects to task planning too, which is where I started. I like thinking about how you combine the structure and reliability of classical planning with the flexibility you get from learned policies, so the system can reason about long-horizon goals without being brittle at the low level.

The other piece I care a lot about is simulation. Robots are slow and break things, so if you want to learn at scale, you need good simulated environments and a way to build large, diverse datasets of behaviors. Designing those environments and the benchmarks around them is less glamorous than a demo video, but I think it's one of the places where the field actually moves forward, because it lets people compare methods honestly.

If I had to sum it up, I'd say I'm drawn to the problem of making robots that can be taught rather than programmed. That means thinking about learning, planning, data, and the human on the other side of the interaction all at once, and that combination is what keeps me in it.
